items.title: Fed's 1y1y pricing says traders want 2015-2019-level tightening — even though inflation isn't 2015-2019
items.idea: Warsh delivered the first hike and, contrary to consensus expecting him to hedge, out-hawked pricing: the curve flattened aggressively, the dollar rallied and vol got crushed. 1y1y Fed Funds now implies 81bps of further tightening, matching the average pace of the 2015-2019 hiking cycle, even though inflation is running hotter now than then. The Fed's own forecast doesn't see 2% inflation until 2029.
items.angle: Paper Alfa raises the pre-2022-midterms 75bp hike precedent as a comp — worth tracking the October-hike-probability debate through a midterm-timing lens, not just a data-dependency one.
items.tweetA: Fed's 1y1y pricing implies 81bps more tightening — same magnitude as the entire 2015-2019 hiking cycle. Except inflation wasn't the problem back then and the Fed's own forecast doesn't see 2% until 2029. The market isn't pricing a soft landing, it's pricing a multi-year slog.
items.tweetB: Everyone expected Warsh to hedge and underdeliver on hawkishness. He didn't — curve flattened, DXY ripped, vol got crushed. That's not what a Fed chair trying to avoid midterm blowback does. Worth asking who's more constrained here: inflation, or the White House's patience.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Simon White/Bloomberg)
items.title: $830B basis trade is the real tail risk in Treasuries, not AI
items.idea: Hedge funds are the marginal Treasury buyer via the basis trade, sized near $830B as of September 2025 — but futures positioning shows funds already trimming exposure. Rising bond vol raises margin, repo and collateral costs fast enough to break the trade's economics, creating a feedback loop: higher yields, higher vol, less hedge-fund demand, then still higher yields to attract the next buyer.
items.angle: This is a structural fragility indicator independent of the Fed's hiking path — worth watching swap spreads and repo stress as a leading signal alongside the rate-pricing story from Paper Alfa and Deutsche Bank elsewhere in this window.
items.tweetA: $830B levered basis trade is now the Treasury market's marginal buyer. That's not real demand, it's a repo-funded bet on convergence. When vol rises enough to blow out margins, that 'buyer' disappears exactly when the Fed is trying to hike into a thinner bond market.
items.tweetB: Forget AI capex funding worries — the actual fragile leverage sitting in markets right now is $830B of basis trade on hedge fund balance sheets. Treasury buybacks can paper over the liquidity gap. They can't replace it if RV funds keep de-grossing.

items.title: A GW of AI data center power costs $5B — and pays for itself in weeks
items.idea: SemiAnalysis tracks 75GW of firm, binding behind-the-meter power orders for AI data centers, with ~20GW ordered in Q2 2026 alone — versus the entire US grid adding only 53GW of generating capacity in all of 2025. A 1GW power plant costs roughly $5B, but that gigawatt can generate about $100B a year in inference revenue at high gross margins, so paying twice as much for power or eating efficiency losses is a rounding error against getting GPUs online a year sooner.
items.angle: This is the clearest read yet on why hyperscaler capex keeps looking 'irrational' to public-market analysts — the ROI math on speed dwarfs the power-cost premium, so expect BTM gas-engine, turbine and fuel-cell suppliers to keep printing order backlogs.
items.tweetA: 75GW of firm behind-the-meter orders vs 53GW the ENTIRE US grid added in 2025. AI labs are out-building the national grid by themselves, one gas plant at a time, because $5B for a GW of power against $100B/year of inference revenue isn't a cost decision, it's a rounding error.
items.tweetB: Turbine delivery slots are sold out past 2030 and now trade on a secondary market at a premium — that's a supply-chain signal equity analysts modeling 'AI capex intensity' are missing entirely. The bottleneck isn't chips anymore, it's turbine backlog.

items.title: China added 10x the power capacity the US did in 2025 — and that's the AI race the chip-export debate misses
items.idea: China added 543GW of generating capacity in 2025 (315GW of it solar) versus the US's 53GW — a 10-to-1 gap — and China has added more capacity since 2021 than the entire US grid contains. China's electricity demand grew 5% to 10,573 TWh versus the US's 3% growth to 4,536 TWh; China's single-year increase alone, roughly 500 TWh, is about what all of Texas uses. Export controls constrain China's chip access, but nothing constrains its power access.
items.angle: The chip-export-control frame ignores that power, not silicon, may be the actual long-run constraint on total AI compute deployed — and on that axis China isn't behind, it's ahead by an order of magnitude.
items.tweetA: China added 543GW of power capacity in 2025. The US added 53GW. That's not a rounding difference, that's a 10x gap in the one input GPUs can't run without. Export controls slow China's chip access. Nothing slows its access to electrons.
items.tweetB: The AI race framing is 'who has better chips.' The actual framing should be 'who can turn on more gigawatts.' China's single-year electricity demand growth alone equals all of Texas's usage. When the constraint shifts from silicon to power, the scoreboard flips.

items.title: Texas paused ALL new data center grid connections after requests hit 474GW — 5x the state's peak demand
items.idea: ERCOT's interconnection queue swelled to about 474GW of requests, more than five times Texas's record peak demand, roughly 90% of it data centers — prompting Governor Abbott to pause new connections in August for a statewide audit. SemiAnalysis reads the pause as bullish for behind-the-meter build-out, since a self-powered campus can promise a hyperscaler a timeline the grid physically cannot.
items.angle: Grid interconnection scarcity is becoming a de facto industrial-policy lever — watch which states position themselves (favorable permitting, cheap gas, a single pipeline regulator) as the next BTM host, with Texas the current leader by design.
items.tweetA: 474GW of interconnection requests in Texas. Peak demand is under 90GW. The state didn't run out of power, it ran out of queue slots — and 90% of the requests are data centers. This is what happens when one industry's capex cycle outpaces every grid planning assumption ever made.
items.tweetB: Texas pausing grid connections is being read as bearish for AI buildout. It's the opposite — it's the strongest argument yet for behind-the-meter gas, because a self-powered campus can promise hyperscalers a timeline the grid physically cannot deliver.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid / Bloomberg's Simon White)
items.title: DB's historical model says this hiking cycle should be 200bps, not the fraction currently priced
items.idea: Deutsche Bank's Jim Reid built a best-fit historical relationship between starting inflation and first-year tightening; with CPI at 3.55%, that model implies slightly over 200bps of hikes in year one, far more than markets are pricing. Bloomberg's Simon White separately argues via neutral-rate math that current pricing may not create enough restrictiveness to actually suppress persistent inflation. Two different methodologies point the same direction: the market is underpricing the terminal rate, not just misjudging meeting timing.
items.angle: If both the historical-analogue model and the neutral-rate model point the same direction, the asymmetric trade is long rate vol or short the front end rather than debating October versus December timing.
items.tweetA: Deutsche Bank's historical model says a 3.55% CPI starting point implies 200bps of year-one hikes. The market is pricing a fraction of that. Two totally different approaches — historical pattern-matching and neutral-rate math — landing on the same number: terminal rate is priced too low, not just too early.
items.tweetB: Everyone's debating October vs December for the next hike. Wrong question. The real mispricing is the destination, not the calendar — if Reid's regression holds, we're maybe a third of the way through this cycle, not near the end.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (FX Daily Hot Take)
items.title: BoJ hiked to a 3-decade high and the yen sold off anyway — the 7-2 vote split is the real story
items.idea: The BoJ raised rates to 1.25%, the highest in more than three decades, yet USD/JPY rallied because the move was fully priced and the Fed had just reset hawkish. The vote split 7-2, with both dissenters — appointed by PM Takaichi — arguing even this hike came too soon. That is the opposite of the signal the yen needed: evidence the BoJ could accelerate the pace between hikes.
items.angle: A hawkish-in-isolation central bank decision that reads dovish in relative terms is a classic setup for continued yen weakness and carry-trade persistence — worth pairing with the Simon White basis-trade item above, since both are about relative-value flows unwinding slower than headline rates suggest.
items.tweetA: BoJ hikes to a 30-year high. Yen sells off. That's not a contradiction, it's FX doing FX things — it trades the surprise, not the level. Two Takaichi-appointed board members dissenting because even this hike was 'too soon' is the opposite of what a currency needing acceleration wanted to hear.
items.tweetB: The BoJ's problem is self-inflicted: telegraph every hike so well that by the time it lands, there's no information left in it. Now Ueda has to surprise through forward guidance alone, and a 7-2 split with dovish dissent is a bad place to start that job from.

items.title: Sell-side has called Strait of Hormuz 'normalization' wrong four times running — and keeps making the same modeling error
items.idea: Goldman has repeatedly forecast Hormuz normalization for specific dates — April, May, June and July — and missed every time, per HFIR. The author's thesis is that no oil model works without first answering 'how does the Iran/US war end,' and sell-side avoids that question because answering it honestly (region stays disrupted, no quick fix) would put a firm at odds with the administration's messaging.
items.angle: This is a case study in sell-side model bias under political pressure — when a research desk can't ask the load-bearing question, every downstream forecast (oil supply, freight, insurance) inherits the same blind spot. Worth cross-referencing against actual tanker/AIS data rather than bank base cases.
items.tweetA: Goldman has called Hormuz 'normalizing by X date' four separate times this year. Wrong every time. Not because the analysts are dumb — because the honest answer to 'how does this war end' is one no bank wants to publish while the White House is watching.
items.tweetB: The oil market's forecasting problem isn't a data problem, it's a permission problem. Every sell-side model assumes the conflict resolves on schedule because modeling 'it doesn't' is the one conclusion nobody's allowed to write down.

items.source: Dark Side of the Boom (Goldman Sachs / Lina Thomas)
items.title: Goldman cuts its 2026 gold target by $250 but holds $5,400 for 2027 — the Fed changes the speed, not the destination
items.idea: Goldman trimmed its year-end-2026 gold fair value to $4,650 from $4,900 after adding an October hike to its Fed path, but kept its $5,400/toz end-2027 target intact because the central-bank-buying nowcast (91 tonnes/month currently, assumed to average 60 tonnes/month through 2026-2027) does the structural work regardless of near-term rate moves. Downside risk to $4,070 exists under a much more hawkish Fed, but call-option demand running about 3x the historical average adds convexity that could amplify any rally via dealer hedging.
items.angle: The interesting number isn't the price target, it's the central-bank-buying assumption of 60 tonnes/month — that's a demand floor priced independent of Fed policy, decoupling gold's 2027 story from the rate-hike debate dominating every other macro item this window.
items.tweetA: Goldman just added a Fed hike to its base case and cut its 2026 gold call by $250 — and left the 2027 target at $5,400 completely unchanged. When a bank can absorb more hawkishness without touching the terminal price, the driver isn't rates anymore, it's central bank buying running at 91 tonnes a month.
items.tweetB: Gold call-option demand is running roughly 3x its historical average right now. That's not a hedge, that's dealers positioning for convexity on the upside. Everyone's watching the Fed for gold's next move — the options desk is watching something else.

items.source: McKinsey (Michael Chui, Roger Roberts, Tanguy Catlin)
items.title: McKinsey's 2026 tech-trends list spans agentic AI to quantum — the signal is what they're telling leaders to ignore, not chase
items.idea: McKinsey's annual technology trends report sorts 14 trends, from agentic AI to cybersecurity to quantum computing, into a triage framework of where to act, invest, or simply keep watching — implying most enterprises are over-indexed on the 'act now' trends and under-prepared on the 'keep watching' ones like quantum.
items.angle: The valuable data point buried in a McKinsey roundup is usually the triage framework itself, not the trend list — worth reading which trends get sorted into 'watch' vs 'act,' since that's effectively McKinsey telling clients where not to spend budget this year.
items.tweetA: McKinsey put quantum computing on the same 2026 trend list as agentic AI. The interesting part isn't that it's on the list, it's which bucket they sorted it into — 'watch,' not 'act.' That's a quiet signal that quantum ROI timelines are still longer than the hype cycle suggests.
items.tweetB: Every consultancy publishes a trends list every year. The useful read isn't the 14 items, it's the triage: what gets 'invest now' vs 'keep watching.' That's effectively McKinsey telling their whole client base where budget should NOT go in 2026.

items.source: McKinsey (Ani Kelkar, Mark Patel — McKinsey Live webinar)
items.title: Humanoid robots will be just 2% of physical AI's value by 2045, per McKinsey — so where's the other 98%?
items.idea: McKinsey's physical AI webinar argues humanoid robots, despite dominating headlines and VC dollars, are expected to capture only about 2% of the physical AI sector's total value by 2045, meaning the 'hidden value pools' leaders are missing sit somewhere else entirely — likely fixed automation, logistics and non-humanoid robotics.
items.angle: This directly undercuts the humanoid-robotics venture narrative that has driven a huge share of 2025-2026 robotics funding — if McKinsey's split is right, the capital allocation and the value pool are pointed in opposite directions.
items.tweetA: Humanoid robots equal 2% of physical AI's value by 2045, per McKinsey. Yet they're getting what looks like the vast majority of robotics VC headlines this cycle. Either McKinsey's model is wrong, or a huge amount of capital is chasing the smallest slice of the pie.
items.tweetB: Nobody's asking where the other 98% of physical AI value sits if it's not humanoids. That's the actual investable question buried in this webinar — non-humanoid industrial automation is the unsexy trade nobody's pricing.

items.title: Only 6% of companies see significant EBIT impact from AI, per McKinsey — the spend-value gap is now a governance problem
items.idea: McKinsey frames the gap between AI spend and realized EBIT impact — just 6% of companies see significant impact — as no longer a technology problem but a governance one, arguing that closing it requires weighing agentic AI's cost against the true cost of the human work it actually replaces, not against hype-cycle expectations.
items.angle: This is the concrete data point that should temper every 'AI is eating jobs and margins' narrative — the ROI simply isn't showing up yet for 94% of companies, a much more interesting and underreported story than the capex headlines dominating the AI-infra item above.
items.tweetA: 6% of companies see significant EBIT impact from AI spend. Hyperscalers are spending like it's an arms race and inference revenue is scaling into the hundreds of billions at the infra layer — but at the actual enterprise adoption level, 94% of companies aren't seeing the P&L show up yet. That gap is the real AI story right now.
items.tweetB: Compare this to the AI infra buildout: labs and hyperscalers are burning billions per gigawatt because inference revenue justifies it at their scale. Meanwhile 94% of enterprise AI deployments can't show EBIT impact. Two completely different AI economies running in parallel.

items.title: McKinsey: energy system 'shock absorbers are thinning' even as it proves resilient through the Hormuz crisis
items.idea: McKinsey Global Institute argues the energy system has weathered the Strait of Hormuz disruption better than expected structurally, but the buffers that enabled that resilience — spare capacity, strategic reserves, alternative routing — are being drawn down, meaning the system has less room to absorb the next shock.
items.angle: This is the structural companion piece to HFIR's tactical oil-endgame item above — HFIR argues sell-side mis-times the resolution, McKinsey argues even if it resolves, the system emerges structurally weaker and more exposed to the next disruption.
items.tweetA: McKinsey's read on Hormuz: the energy system held up better than feared, but the shock absorbers that made that possible are thinning out. That's a very different risk statement than 'the crisis is over' — it's 'the next one hits harder.'
items.tweetB: Pair this with HFIR's point that sell-side keeps calling Hormuz 'resolved' on a rolling basis: even McKinsey, writing from a much more neutral seat, is saying the resilience was real but non-repeatable at the same cost. The next disruption doesn't get the same buffer.
